name: open-simh
why: Boot real PDP, VAX, and other vintage machines in software and poke at operating systems from the era.

brief.what_it_is: Open SIMH is a family of software simulators of historic computers, built as one framework (SCP) with many machine-specific simulator programs. The brew package ships 24 executables, including altair, pdp1, pdp8, pdp10, pdp11, vax, vax780, sigma, i7094 and b5500-era families, though the list of machines is not all covered in the README. Each simulator emulates the hardware of one machine so that its original operating system and software can run unchanged; the homepage cites Version 7 Unix (1979) running on it. Per the status document, disk and tape images (raw disks, virtual disk containers, AWS and TAR tapes) are attached to the simulated devices, and console I/O goes to your terminal or a TELNET port, with optional SDL2 video windows.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames the goal as preserving knowledge held in old software by providing the ability to execute and experience it through simulation of the original hardware. The README describes SIMH as created by Bob Supnik, originally at Digital Equipment Corporation, and extended by many contributors.
brief.how_it_works: Each simulator emulates a specific machine's CPU and devices in software and runs the period operating system from disk or tape images. The shared SCP command layer provides the console prompt, ATTACH/DETACH of media, BOOT and breakpoint handling, and scripting through DO files, EXPECT and SEND. The README does not spell out the emulation internals beyond this.

commands_seen.context: Build command from the README for compiling one simulator from source with GNU make, for example vax; the simulator name is a placeholder.
Installs the VDE networking library on macOS via Homebrew, one of the optional dependencies for Ethernet support; the README also lists sdl2 and sdl2_ttf.
Ubuntu package for libpcap, one of the Linux dependencies listed for building simulators with networking and video support.
Example from the README defining a command alias through an environment variable; afterwards typing say Hello there prints Hello there.
Enables the remote console facility on a TELNET port so out-of-band commands can be entered into a running simulator.
Lists the devices and features of the running simulator, per the command reference in the status document.
Shows the built-in per-device help, per the status document; variants include HELP dev ATTACH and HELP dev REGISTERS.
Throttles the simulator by t milliseconds every x cycles, per the SCP command list in the status document.

brief.install_notes: The README says to git clone the open-simh/simh master branch and run make with the simulator name, and that GNU make is required (gmake on some systems). Ethernet-capable simulators (the VAX and PDP-11 families) need extra networking components; the README points to a 0readme_ethernet.txt file for these. Optional packages (vde2, libsdl2, libsdl2_ttf, libpcap, libpcre, libedit) add networking and video; without them the build succeeds with reduced functionality. Windows builds use Visual Studio 2008 through 2019 or MinGW32, with steps in a Visual Studio Projects readme. The homepage has Download links for tar, zip and source, and the TOC mentions prebuilt Windows simulators, but I did not read those pages.
brief.standout: Beyond running old systems, the project has a scripting layer for the simulator console: DO command files with labels, GOTO, IF, ON error traps, EXPECT/SEND for automating a login prompt, and a remote TELNET console for changing a running machine. Its SHOW and SET commands cover asynchronous I/O, throttling and clock calibration, and it also simulates some uncommon hardware, such as the Sigma, SDS 940 and AT&T 3B2 families.
brief.status: Unknown as to release dates and recent commits: I saw no last-release date or commit date. The README is current in tone, the status document is labelled as v4.0 current with a 19-01 date, and the page has a Coverity Scan badge. The homepage says the project is run by dedicated volunteers. Treat it as active but unconfirmed.
brief.caveats: The README says the project is MIT licensed, but I did not read the LICENSE text. Windows is supported via Visual Studio or MinGW32; MinGW64 is explicitly not supported and Cygwin is not the preferred option with fewer features. The Ethernet and video features depend on host libraries and may be missing if they are not installed. The homepage disclaims guarantees and says the information is provided at your own risk. The README asks contributors not to copy code from github.com/simh/simh unless they wrote it, which marks a split from an earlier codebase as of 12 May 2022.
quotes: SIMH is a framework and family of computer simulators, initiated by Bob Supnik and continued with contributions (large and small) from many others.

judge.reason: Booting unchanged vintage operating systems on simulated PDP, VAX, and other hardware makes computing history tangible and invites hands-on exploration.

entry.title: Open SIMH
entry.tldr: A family of simulators that boot historic computers like the PDP-8, PDP-11 and VAX in software, so their original operating systems run unchanged.
entry.deeper_look:
Open SIMH is one framework with many machine-specific simulators. Each one emulates the CPU and devices of a single historic machine, such as a PDP-1, PDP-8, PDP-10, PDP-11, VAX, Altair or SDS 940. The original operating system and software then run as they did on the real hardware. The homepage notes that Version 7 Unix, released in 1979, "runs unchanged today on SimH".

The simulators share a command layer called SCP. At its `sim>` prompt you attach disk and tape images to simulated devices, boot, set breakpoints, and inspect the machine with SHOW and HELP. Console I/O goes to your terminal or to a TELNET port, and some simulators can open an SDL2 video window. Scripting is built in: DO files with labels, GOTO, IF and ON error traps, plus EXPECT and SEND for automating a login prompt.

The homepage describes the aim as preserving the knowledge held in old software by letting people execute and experience it on simulated original hardware. SIMH was started by Bob Supnik, originally at Digital Equipment Corporation, and extended by many contributors. This Open SIMH repository dates from a split from an earlier codebase in May 2022.

The idea underneath is that a computer is a specification you can run. Once a machine is simulated, its operating system, its quirks and its front-panel conventions become things you can poke at, and the SHOW commands help you see what the hardware was made of.
entry.install:
brew install open-simh
# Ethernet and video support rely on host libraries (vde, libpcap, SDL2). You also need disk or tape images of the operating system you want to boot, which the package does not supply.

try_this.what_happens: Starts the PDP-11 simulator binary; the brief does not confirm that this flag is supported, so start it without arguments for the sim> prompt if it fails.
At the sim> prompt, shows built-in help for a device; HELP dev ATTACH and HELP dev REGISTERS go deeper.
At the sim> prompt, lists the devices and features of the running simulator.

entry.whats_unique: It covers dozens of machines under one command interface, including rarities like the SDS 940, Sigma and AT&T 3B2 families. It runs the original period software unchanged rather than imitating it.
entry.caveats: The package installs only the simulators; you have to find bootable disk or tape images yourself, and the brief could not confirm recent release or commit dates.
